title: Reorder List
description: Brute force to optimized: an array with alternating front/back indices versus an in-place find-middle, reverse-second-half, weave-together technique.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln-1 -> Ln, reorder it to become: L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... You may not modify the values in the list's nodes (only the pointers may change).

blocks.caption: Split the list at the middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together alternately

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a singly linked list"],["Output","The same list, in place, reordered to alternate between the front and back halves"],["Goal","Achieve the front/back alternating reorder using O(1) extra space (no array of all values)"],["Constraints","The number of nodes is in the range [1, 5*10^4]; 1 <= Node.val <= 1000"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The reorder alternates between the FRONT and the BACK of the list","Splitting the list into two halves, reversing the second half (so its own \"front\" becomes what was originally its back), then weaving the two halves together"],["O(1) extra space is the ideal target (no array of all values)","This directly combines three previously-covered techniques in this category: find-the-middle, reverse-a-list, and merge/weave two lists together"]]}

blocks.text: The desired order takes the first node, then the LAST node, then the second node, then the second-to-last node, and so on, alternating from both ends toward the middle.

blocks.title: Analogy: Dealing Cards From Both Ends of a Deck, Alternating
blocks.text: Imagine a deck of cards laid out in a line, and dealing them out by alternating: first from the FRONT of the line, then from the BACK, then front again, then back again, and so on. A clever way to physically achieve this without repeatedly walking to "the back" (slow on a singly linked list) is to first split the line into two halves, flip the second half around (so its former back is now its own front), and then simply weave the two halves together one card at a time.

blocks.caption: The list is split at its middle, the second half is reversed, and the two halves are woven together one node at a time

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Split at middle: first half [1,2], second half [3,4]","Two halves","Standard slow/fast pointer midpoint"],["Reverse second half: [3,4] becomes [4,3]","Reversed second half","Its own front (4) is what was originally the list's true back"],["Weave alternately: 1, 4, 2, 3","[1,4,2,3]","Take one from each half in turn, starting with the first half"]]}

blocks.text: Before extracting every value into an array and manually rebuilding via alternating front/back array indices, notice this problem combines three techniques already mastered elsewhere in this category: find-the-middle, reverse-a-list, and weave-two-lists-together.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The desired output alternates between "next unused node from the front half" and "next unused node from the back half," which is naturally awkward on a singly linked list, since walking backward is not directly possible.

Observation 2: REVERSING the second half of the list converts "walking backward through the back half" into simply "walking forward through the reversed back half," since its own front is now exactly what was originally the list's true tail.

Observation 3: The middle can be found using the exact same slow/fast pointer technique as Middle of the Linked List, splitting the list into a first half and a second half.

Observation 4: With the second half reversed, weaving the two halves together (alternately linking one node from each) directly produces the desired final order, using only pointer re-linking, no extra array.

Recognizing this problem as "find-the-middle + reverse-second-half + weave-together" (three previously mastered sub-techniques combined) is the key insight that makes an otherwise-tricky reordering approachable.
This is a three-phase technique: split at the midpoint, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together one node at a time.
Extract every value into an array, then build the reordered array by alternately taking from the front and back using two index pointers.

items: Walk through the list, collecting every value into an array.
Using two pointers (lo starting at the front, hi starting at the back), alternately append values[lo] (advancing lo) and values[hi] (advancing hi) until they cross.

codes.python:
def reorder_list(values):
    result = []
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    turn = 0
    while lo <= hi:
        if turn % 2 == 0:                                                   # alternate: front of the list, then back of the list
            result.append(values[lo])
            lo += 1
        else:
            result.append(values[hi])
            hi -= 1
        turn += 1
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(reorder_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Alternating lo (front) and hi (back) directly mirrors the required L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, ... output pattern.
The loop naturally terminates once lo and hi cross, correctly handling both even and odd-length inputs (an odd length simply has one final unpaired middle value).

blocks.text: Correctly reproduces the exact alternating front/back order required, since array indexing allows direct O(1) access from both ends.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect plus one to rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array.

Limitation: the O(n) array is unnecessary; splitting, reversing the second half, and weaving the two halves together achieves the identical reordering directly on the existing nodes, in O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force needs O(n) space purely to allow "backward" access. Instead: find the list's middle (slow/fast pointers), split it into two halves, reverse the second half (so its front is now what was originally the tail), then weave the two halves together, alternately taking one node from each.

Phase 1: find the middle using slow/fast pointers (slow ends at the last node of the first half). Phase 2: split (slow.next = null) and reverse the second half. Phase 3: weave, alternately linking first.next = second, second.next = (saved original first.next), advancing both pointers, until the (shorter) second half is exhausted.
Split the list at its middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together one node at a time.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The woven result is [1,5,2,4,3], matching the expected output; the first half's leftover node (3) correctly ends up at the very end.

codes.python:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        next_node = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev = head
        head = next_node
    return prev

def reorder_list(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head

    slow, fast = head, head                                                 # phase 1: find the middle (slow/fast pointers)
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

    second = slow.next                                                      # phase 2: split into two halves, reverse the second
    slow.next = None
    second = reverse(second)

    first = head                                                            # phase 3: weave the two halves together, alternating
    while second:
        t1, t2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = t1
        first, second = t1, t2
    return head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    reorder_list(head)
    values = []
    node = head
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each phase (find middle, reverse, weave) is a single linear pass.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes throughout.

After reversing the second half, walking it FORWARD is equivalent to walking the original list BACKWARD from its true tail, which is exactly the access pattern the reordering needs. The weave step alternately attaches one node from each half, always saving the "next" pointer of the CURRENT first-half node before overwriting it, since that saved pointer is needed to continue the first half's own chain in the next iteration.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Odd total length","The first half naturally ends up with one extra node (the true middle), which simply becomes the final unpaired node at the very end"],["Even total length","Both halves have equal length, and every node from the first half gets paired with one from the second"],["Second half becomes exhausted (second is null)","The weave loop stops, since every node from the second half has already been placed"]]}

items: The middle-finding loop condition (fast.next and fast.next.next) is specifically chosen so slow lands on the LAST node of the first half (giving the first half the extra node for odd lengths), matching the required output pattern.
reverse() is the exact same standard iterative reversal used elsewhere in this category, applied only to the second half.
The weave loop carefully saves BOTH t1 (first's original next) and t2 (second's original next) before any reassignment, since both original chains must continue being walked correctly.

blocks.text: Any reordering that needs alternating "front" and "back" access on a singly linked list can often be achieved in O(1) extra space by reversing the back portion first, converting the awkward backward access into simple forward access, then weaving the two portions together.

items: Forgetting to save BOTH halves' original "next" pointers before reassigning them during the weave step, losing track of one chain.
Getting the middle-finding loop condition slightly wrong, causing the two halves to be split at the wrong point (off by one node).
Attempting to weave without first reversing the second half, which would require backward traversal that a singly linked list cannot efficiently support.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single node","Returned unchanged; the base case check (head or head.next is null) handles this directly"],["Exactly two nodes","The first half is just the first node, the second half just the second; weaving simply swaps nothing (already in the desired alternating order)"],["Odd-length list","The first half naturally receives the extra middle node, which correctly ends up unpaired at the very end of the result"]]}

items: Explicitly naming the three sub-techniques being combined (find-the-middle, reverse, weave-together) up front demonstrates the pattern-composition skill this problem is specifically designed to test.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reorder alternating FRONT and BACK" on a singly linked list points toward reversing the back half first (converting backward access into forward access), then weaving the two halves together.

items: How would you verify the middle-finding step lands on the correct split point for BOTH even and odd lengths? Trace the slow/fast pointer loop condition explicitly on both a 4-node and a 5-node example.

Could this be done recursively instead? Yes, though the iterative three-phase approach is generally preferred for its clean O(1) extra space, since a naive recursive approach would use O(n) stack space.

How does this connect to Palindrome Linked List, which also uses find-middle and reverse-second-half? Both problems share the exact same first two phases; this problem's final phase WEAVES the halves together, while the palindrome check's final phase simply COMPARES them.

Directly combines the find-the-middle technique from Middle of the Linked List, the standard iterative reversal from Reverse Linked List, and shares its first two phases with Palindrome Linked List elsewhere in this category.
